ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study obtained ethical approval from the University of Toronto and the University of Pennsylvania research ethics boards, as well as the Nigerian Ahmadu Bello University Teaching Hospital Shika Health Research Ethics Committee (#ABUTHZ/HREC/G55/2026).
Ethics approval statement: Ethics approval (ID #46237) was received from the University of Toronto Institutional Review Board on April 18, 2024.

All child participants completed language and literacy measures in both the first language of literacy (i.e., either Hausa or Kanuri) and the second language of literacy (i.e., English), as well as language environment questions.
However, only 180 participants completed the language and literacy measures in Kanuri, whereas the remaining participants (N = 1415) completed the measures in Hausa.

The observed lower English PA scores are likely explained by a lack of pre-displacement school enrollment (where children would be exposed to the English language), compounded with the paucity of literacy instruction that children who were enrolled in school were exposed to.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A power analysis was run using the pwr package in R (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=h4oDHI) to determine the required sample size to answer the research questions. Assuming α = 0.05, f² = 0.20 (between small [0.15] and medium [0.35] effect sizes), power (1-b) = 0.8, and 7 predictors in the model (including 3 covariates), a sample size of 71 was considered adequate. In the Kanuri readers group, however, only 20 participants scored above a zero on at least one of the literacy tasks in Kanuri, and only 55 participants scored above a zero on at least one of the literacy tasks in English (see supplementary materials Figure 1). Therefore, we were underpowered to detect effects of within-and across-language predictors of Kanuri literacy outcomes and English literacy outcomes in the Kanuri readers group, and excluded this sample in analyses of literacy outcomes. Comparatively, in the Hausa readers group, 570 participants scored above a zero on at least one of the literacy tasks in Hausa, and 659 participants scored above a zero on at least one of the literacy tasks in English (see supplementary materials Figure 1). Therefore, we had enough power to detect effects of within-and across-language predictors of Hausa literacy outcomes and English literacy outcomes in the Hausa readers group.

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Internally-displaced children often lack schooling and reside in highly multilingual contexts.
In Nigeria, children must learn to read in a local language (e.g., Hausa), and English; here, language skills can transfer across languages to support biliteracy.
Importantly, the strength of transfer is constrained by proficiency in language skills.
Formal schooling and early life exposure are crucial for acquisition of language skills.

In our sample of 1595 Nigerian internally-displaced children, we investigated how pre-displacement school enrollment and early life language language exposure (i.e., at home) predict language skills, and how language skills transfer across languages to support literacy.
Pre-displacement school enrollment particularly supported phonological awareness, and early life language exposure particularly supported vocabulary.
Phonological awareness was stronger in Hausa relative to English, resulting in greater transfer from Hausa to English.
IDP context allows the investigation of cognition and environment to enrich theoretical models of biliteracy, and inform pedagogical practices.
Education is a powerful tool for improving children's academic, social, and economic prospects.
However, global access to schooling remains deeply unequal, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa, where 98.4 million children are out of school (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?5Lgc9j.

text.text: Resource-constrained, conflict-afflicted, multilingual contexts are rarely considered in the literature on literacy acquisition.
Here, we investigate how children living in IDP camps learn to read in two languages.

Biliteracy in IDP contexts can be examined through the Component Model of Reading, which posits that the acquisition of literacy skills is supported by cognitive, ecological (i.e., context-dependent), and psychological factors (Aaron et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Biliteracy in IDP contexts can be examined through the Component Model of Reading, which posits that the acquisition of literacy skills is supported by cognitive, ecological (i.e., context-dependent), and psychological factors <ref type="bibr">(Aaron et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we focus on cognitive and ecological predictors of letter-and word-level reading skills (i.e., emergent reading skills).

Learning to read involves mapping graphemes to phonemes and combining these phonemes into words to access meaning (Hulme, 2002) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=1EPP7z i.e., the orthography -phonologysemantics pathway, as described in the Triangle Model of reading (Harm & Seidenberg, 2004; Snow, 2006).

text.text: Emergent reading is highly predicted by phonological awareness (PA), that is, the ability to recognize and manipulate sound structures at different levels of granularity (e.g., phonemic vs syllabic) in a language (Wagner & Torgesen, 1987).

text.text: As word reading becomes more automatichttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=S3q9T3 readers can also access a word's meaning directly from its orthographic form and with less reliance on decoding (Harm & Seidenberg, 2004) , a process known as direct lexical access (i.e., orthography-semantics pathway).

text.text: This type of word recognition is typically more robustly predicted by vocabulary than it is by PA, as experienced readers can access semantic information more automatically from a word's orthographic form (Anderson & Freebody, 1983; Berends & Reitsma, 2006; Harm & Seidenberg, 2004).

text.text: Language skills also support reading skills cross-linguistically (Chung et al., 2019; Durgunoğlu et al., 1993; Geva & Ryan, 1993; Haigh et al., 2011; Keung & Ho, 2009; Wang et al., 2006).

text.text: Cross-linguistic transfer is the ability of language skills in one language to facilitate the acquisition of literacy in the other language(s) (Odlin, 1989).

text.text: Importantly, there is significantly less evidence for transfer of vocabulary relative to evidence for transfer of PA.

Transfer of vocabulary skills is often limited to etymologically similar languages (i.e., through cognate awareness) and is often task-dependent (Chung et al., 2019a; Lindsey et al., 2003; Ordóñez et al., 2002; Raudszus et al., 2018).

text.text: Comparatively, robust evidence exists for the transfer of PA across both typologically similar and distant languages, and regardless of differences in tasks (Chung et al., 2019a; Dixon et al., 2025; Gottardo et al., 2023; Jasińska et al., 2019; Ordóñez et al., 2002; Veii & Everatt, 2005).

(2025) found that children's PA skills in L1 (Hausa) predicted decoding skills in L2 (English), despite differences in orthographic transparency (i.e., English is opaque whereas Hausa is transparent), and less than 50% overlap in their phonemic inventories (Muhammad-Gombe, 2019).

text.text: Cross-linguistic transfer direction and strength are highly dependent on ecological factors that contribute to proficiency in the language of transfer (Chung et al., 2019a).

text.text: For instance, where L2 proficiency is greater, transfer is often observed from L2 to L1 (e.g., Chung et al., 2018; Pasquarella et al., 2011); and where L1 and L2 proficiency is similar, bidirectional transfer is observed (e.g., Deacon et al., 2007; Deacon et al., 2009).

text.text: Students exposed to the language of literacy early in life (i.e., at home) demonstrate better overall language proficiency, which can support greater language transfer (Altman et al., 2014; Deacon et al., 2007; Flores et al., 2017; Huang & Choi, 2026; Jasińska & Petitto, 2018; Kim & Piper, 2019; Pham & Tipton, 2018; Rojas et al., 2016; Rydland & Grøver, 2021; Sorenson Duncan & Paradis, 2020).

text.text: The development of literacy-related language skills is further supported by formal schooling and literacy instruction.

PA and literacy are reciprocally linked; children's PA improves with greater exposure to literacy instruction and mastery of the associations between letters and sounds (Bentin & Leshem, 1993; Eme, 2011; Jasińska et al., 2024; Morais & Kolinsky, 2019).

text.text: Therefore, in-school children generally show greater PA relative to out-of-school children (e.g. see evidence from rural Tanzania; Alcock et al., 2018).

text.text: Moreover, timely enrollment in formal schooling is associated with higher language and literacy proficiency over time; children who enroll in school late show poorer learning outcomes (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=RFjWnc  Alcock et al., 2018; Birdsong & Molis, 2001; Burgess et al., 2002; Chansa-Kabali et al., 2014; Paradis, 2019; van den Bosch et al., 2019; Whitehead et al., 2024).

text.text: Considering that displacement further delays school start for IDPs in Nigeria, with many displaced children instead attending temporary and makeshift educational programs, if any at all, IDPs are likely to experience difficulties in acquiring literacy-related language skills.

In the context of displacementhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=yuwL3l mismatches between the child's first language (i.e., spoken at home; L1) and the language they read in (i.e., here referred to as the language of literacy), and a lack of formal schooling are experiences that may reduce proficiency in language-related literacy skills (Bitetti & Hammer, 2016; Scarpino et al., 2019; Deacon et al., 2013; Hogan et al., 2005; Nagy et al., 1985) , thereby limiting cross-linguistic transfer for biliteracy acquisition.

text.text: The majority of research on biliteracy in displaced children includes children who resettled in middle-and high-income countries (i.e., externally-displaced refugees).

Although these populations similarly show lags in literacy outcomes compared to age-matched peers (Al-Janaideh et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?loLy6M 2023; Kaplan et al., 2016) , the contexts in which many of these resettled refugees acquire literacy differ substantially from those experienced by internally displaced children who reside in majority-world settings.

text.text: For instance, externally-displaced refugees who resettle in European or North-American countries experience relatively stable learning environments (i.e., with little or no more disruptions to schooling) and reside in predominantly monolingual settings (i.e., with a single language of instruction).

Importantly, this body of research does not reflect the global distribution of displaced populations: the majority of refugees are internally displaced in low-income countries, where resources are often constrained, and education systems face greater instability (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=xKwF7Q. Jasińska & Guei, 2022; UNHCR, n.d.-b).

text.text: The contextual differences of internally displaced populations' learning experiences are critical to consider; indeed, recent research suggests that unique displacement-related experiences differentially predict literacy acquisition (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=ilorOC  Akkad & Jasińska, 2026; Gottardo et al., 2023).

text.text: The present study aimed to provide insight into predictors of literacy-related language skills and cross-linguistic transfer in children residing in IDP camps in Northeast Nigeria who were speakers of Hausa or Kanuri as well as English.

We assume context-driven models of literacy and cross-linguistic transfer -i.e., the Component Model of Reading (Aaron et al., 2008a) and the Interactive Transfer Framework (Chung et al., 2019a) and focus on cognitive and ecological predictors of word-level reading skills (i.e., emergent reading skills) in both of a bilingual child's two languages.

text.text: The consideration of ecological predictors of biliteracy is especially important in low-literacy and low-resource contexts, where cognitive predictors of literacy (e.g., PA and vocabulary) may themselves show floor effects (Nag et al., 2024; Whitehead et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The consideration of ecological predictors of biliteracy is especially important in low-literacy and low-resource contexts, where cognitive predictors of literacy (e.g., PA and vocabulary) may themselves show floor effects <ref type="bibr">(Nag et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Whitehead et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We investigated the following research question: How are children's learning experiences in IDP camp contexts (pre-displacement school enrollment, language experiences) related to language skills, and how do these skills predict literacy within-and across-languages (e.g., Hausa → English and English → Hausa)?

In line with the evidence in the literature, we hypothesized that ecological factors including pre-displacement school enrollment and home language experience were related to language and literacy skills.
We predicted that children who received some schooling before displacement and who were exposed to the language of literacy at home would show better PA and vocabulary in that language.
We also hypothesized that the direction (e.g., Hausa → English vs English → Hausa) and strength of cross-linguistic transfer will rely on relative language proficiency.

Considering robust evidence showing that biliteracy acquisition is context-dependent (as motivated by theoretical models of literacy; Aaron et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?lJKfaN 2008; Chung et al., 2019) , it is crucial to examine how the unique and underexplored learning experiences of IDPs (i.e., learning in highly multilingual and low-resource environments) determine predictors of language and literacy skills to inform pedagogical practice and education policy.

text.text: Participants 1595 child participants (male = 627; female = 968) aged 5-15 years and their caregivers (N=1038) participated in the study.
All families resided in IDP camps in Borno, Nigeria.

Data for this study were collected as part of a one-year impact evaluation of the FastTrack intervention, a technology-driven educational intervention for foundational numeracy and literacy skills that ran between April 2025 and April 2026 (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?xVRv4X  Jasińska et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Data for this study were collected as part of a one-year impact evaluation of the FastTrack intervention, a technology-driven educational intervention for foundational numeracy and literacy skills that ran between April 2025 and April 2026 (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?xVRv4X">AREAi, n.d.;</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Jasińska et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Only baseline data (i.e., before treatment assignment) were used in our analyses.

The study obtained ethical approval from the University of Toronto and the University of Pennsylvania research ethics boards, as well as the Nigerian Ahmadu Bello University Teaching Hospital Shika Health Research Ethics Committee (#ABUTHZ/HREC/G55/2026).

Participant oral consent (both informed consent from the caregiver and assent from the child) was obtained by trained staff members in Hausa or Kanuri, and trained AREAi enumerators administered all assessments to participants individually.

All child participants completed language and literacy measures in both the first language of literacy (i.e., either Hausa or Kanuri) and the second language of literacy (i.e., English), as well as language environment questions.
Caregivers completed migration-and education-history questions about their child(ren).
In this sample, 642 participants reported speaking Hausa as their L1, and 879 reported speaking Kanuri as their L1.
However, only 180 participants completed the language and literacy measures in Kanuri, whereas the remaining participants (N = 1415) completed the measures in Hausa.
Of note, many of the participants whose L1 was Kanuri preferred to be assessed in Hausa.

This may be attributed to the fact that Hausa is the lingua franca in Maidaguri, Borno State and children who received any schooling would likely have had Hause as the language of instruction; therefore, native Kanuri speakers' preference for Hausa interaction and assessment with our research team likely reflected a general preference for reading in Hausa, even among those who identified Kanuri as their L1.

text.text: In the initial phoneme identification task, children were asked to listen to a sequence of words and then identify the word that began with a particular sound.

In the initial phoneme deletion task, a word was read aloud and children were asked to repeat this while omitting its initial sound.
For example, in English, "tower" without /t/ is "our".
Children skipped the initial phoneme deletion task if they failed to provide a single correct response on the initial phoneme identification task.

text.text: Children were presented with five words and asked to produce a word with the same meaning (e.g., in English, "jump" for "hop"); and then were presented with five words and asked to produce a word with the opposite meaning (e.g., in English, "no" for "yes").
A composite vocabulary score was computed by summing the scores of the two tasks.

Children were shown a list of letters and asked to provide either the letter's name or sound.
After three practice items with feedback, children read a list of 100 items.
The task ended after one minute or if the child failed to provide a single correct response within the first ten items.
Word reading was assessed with 50 high-frequency words (e.g., in English, "you", "he", "flight"; in Hausa, "ke" (you),"ta" (of), "ina" (I am); in Kanuri, "ti" (body), "balo" (scar), "kora" (big)).
After three practice items, children read aloud as many of these words as they could.
The task ended after one minute or if the child did not provide a single correct response on the first five words.

Non-word reading was assessed using 50 monosyllabic pseudo-words (e.g., in English, "nad", "lus", "dit"; in Hausa, "soto", "lam", "tita"; in Kanuri, "lo", "peke", "kosi") that conformed to the phonotactic rules of each language.
After three practice items with feedback, children read aloud as many of these words as they could.
The task ended after one minute or if the child did not provide a single correct response on the first five words.

To address our research question, we first examined whether pre-displacement school enrollment and early life language exposure (i.e., whether the child spoke the language at home) predicted PA and vocabulary depth in Hausa or Kanuri, and in English.

We then examined how PA and vocabulary predicted within-language reading skills in Hausa, English, and Kanuri; and across-language reading skills in the Hausa-English language pair (see below for discussion of analytic limitation for Kanuri-English).
We examined how PA and vocabulary depth predicted literacy skills as a composite of letter-sound identification, familiar word reading, and nonword reading.

To create the literacy composite, we summed participants' raw scores across letter-sound identification, familiar word reading, and nonword reading (/100 for letter-sound identification; /50 for familiar word and nonword reading).

Summing raw scores instead of averaging or standardizing scores was done to preserve zero-inflated and integer composite values, necessary characteristics of outcome variables in zero-inflated models.
Literacy scores were positively skewed and zero-inflated, as such, zero-inflated regression models were conducted.

When the outcome variable was also significantly overdispersed (as indicated by theta values), zero-inflated negative binomial (NEGBIN) regression models were used; if not significantly overdispersed, zero-inflated Poisson regression models were used, instead.

For an additional check of model choice, the Akaike Information Criteria (AIC) fit index was calculated for both Poisson and NEGBIN versions of each model; the model with the lowest AIC index was selected.
The results of both the count model (i.e., including only non-zero scores) and the zero-inflated model (i.e., including also zero-count scores) were included and interpreted.
Age, MPI, and gender were included in all models as covariates.

For descriptive statistics, participants' scores on PA, vocabulary depth, letter/sound ID, familiar word reading, and nonword reading were divided by the total number of items in each task to derive standard accuracy scores (i.e., 0 to 1) for easier comparisons.
We controlled for the false discovery rate (FDR) across multiple hypothesis testing by adjusting raw p-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (i.e., by extracting q-values).

This study investigated how pre-displacement school enrollment and early life language exposure relate to literacy-related language skills (i.e., PA and vocabulary depth) and cross-linguistic transfer in children residing in IDP camps in Northeast Nigeria.
Overall, our samples of Hausa-English readers and Kanuri-English bilinguals showed very poor language and literacy skills; most participants could not read in either their languages.
Pre-displacement school enrollment and early life language exposure supported literacy-related language skills (i.e., PA and vocabulary depth) in low-literacy and multilingual settings.

We also found that stronger cross-linguistic transfer of PA to emergent literacy skills was observed in the Hausa → English direction relative to the English → Hausa direction, and that Hausa-English readers performed significantly better on Hausa PA relative to English PA.
In line with the general consensus in the literature, Hausa-English readers who had some schooling prior to displacement were advantaged in their literacy-related language skills, particularly in PA.
In our sample of Hausa-English readers, only 24% reported having some schooling prior to displacement.
Nigeria has faced protracted and compounded issues resulting in inaccessible schooling.
Classrooms often do not have enough educational resources and are significantly overcrowded, resulting in ineffective instruction (Adekola, 2007; Bolaji et al., 2019; Boulton et al., 2009).

In line with the general evidence in the literature, Hausa-English readers who had early life exposure to Hausa (i.e., spoke it at home) were advantaged in their Hausa literacy-related language skills, particularly their Hausa vocabulary depth (Daskalaki et al., 2020; Gagarina & Klassert, 2018; Jia et al., 2014; Jia & Paradis, 2020).

text.text: Importantly, early life language exposure was also positively related to PA in Hausa-English readers attesting to the relevance of early life language exposure in preparing children for literacy skills acquisition.
Exposure to the language of literacy only at an older age is characteristic of other low-resource and highly multilingual contexts where children can experience delayed school starts.

For example, in Côte d'Ivoire, many children start school at a later age (Gulematova et al., 2016), delaying their exposure to the language of literacy, and impacting the acquisition of literacy-related language skills (Brice et al., 2024; Whitehead et al., 2024; Jasińska et al., 2024; Hannon et al., 2025).

Hausa PA, but not Hausa vocabulary depth, was associated with Hausa literacy, and both English PA and English vocabulary depth were associated with English literacy.
Of note, the strength of association between Hausa PA and Hausa literacy was stronger than that of English PA and English literacy.
Relatedly, children scored significantly better on PA in Hausa relative to English.

These results attest to the role of PA as a foundational skill in literacy acquisition, with a particular relevance in early literacy achievement (Bentin & Leshem, 1993; Calfee et al., 1973; Ehri et al., 200; Eme, 2011; Jasińska et al., 2024; Lonigan et al., 2000; Morais & Kolinsky, 2019; Torgesen et al., 1994; Wagner et al., 1997).

Moreover, studying the educational experiences of displaced children provides us with unique opportunities to advance the evidence base of models of reading and cross-linguistic transfer.

Specifically, the educational experiences of displaced children provided evidence into the role of contextual variables (e.g., lack of schooling and early life language exposure) into the acquisition of literacy-related language skills, as suggested by the Component Model of Reading.

Additionally, investigating a context where children learn to read in two languages and in a linguistically diverse setting provides insight into the dynamics of cross-linguistic transfer (i.e., its direction and strength) and how these dynamics rely on relative proficiency in the language pair, as suggested by the Interactive Transfer Framework (Chung et al., 2019a).

Considering our sample did not show enough variance in their language and literacy scores, as evident in the highly zero-inflated distributions, our models could not account for additional variance contributed by IDP camp name or family identification.

Future research looking into post-intervention outcomes (which are likely to have less zero-inflated distributions) could investigate whether these contexts further distinguish children in their educational outcomes.

Additionally, although our analysis of internal consistency showed good overall reliability for the English, Hausa, and Kanuri language measures, this high internal consistency might be due to many participants scoring zero on most items in all tasks at baseline.

In other words, zero inflation is likely to reduce variability in the participants' scores, resulting in no directionality in associations between measures as well as high correlations in item statistics.
Future research should continue to examine internal consistency of measures in samples with wider skill ranges.

This study explored how unique learning experiences of internally displaced children relate to language skills, and how these language skills support emergent literacy skills withinand across-languages.

Schooling and early life language exposure to the languages that children have to read in are crucial for the acquisition of language and literacy skills, but are not common experiences for children in IDP camps.
With limited language skills, children in IDP camps show high rates of illiteracy and low literacy skills.
Despite overall poor language skills, children show cross-linguistic support for literacy, attesting to the role of cross-linguistic support for biliteracy acquisition.

text.text: More than 40% of children globally lack access to education in the language they speak at home and understand fluently, more frequently in low-resource and highly multilingual settings their less proficient language.
Our findings provide novel insight into biliteracy development in low-resource and highly-multilingual contexts, and inform the relatively scarce evidence-base of the Interactive Transfer Framework.
Finally, our study motivates the need for additional investigation into how underexplored, but widespread learning experiences relate to children's education outcomes in similar contexts and beyond.
